newsitem.title: CANADA: New Abitibi looks to Asia for market growth.
newsitem.headline: New Abitibi looks to Asia for market growth.

text.p: The new company that would be formed by the proposed merger of Abitibi-Price Inc and Stone-Consolidated Corp would look to Asia for growth in newsprint markets, its incoming president said on Monday.

At a press conference to provide details on the merger, James Doughan, president and chief executive officer of Stone-Consolidated, who would keep those titles at the new company, Abitibi-Consolidated, said Asia holds the biggest promise for growth in newsprint consumption.
Demand in North America, meanwhile, will be flat or "even down" in the years ahead, he said.
"By the turn of the century, there are going to be a billion middle-class Asians. If we can get them reading like the (South) Koreans, we will be running out of newsprint shortly," Doughan said.
Doughan said that of the merged company's 4.4 million tonnes of annual production capacity for all publication grade papers, 1.2 million tonnes would be sold "outside of North America."
"We look at the North American market as flat or static, or even down, but we still look at the total overall growth of newsprint (consumption) as very positive," Doughan said.

He said some estimates are that South Korean consumption of newsprint grew by 35 percent last year and despite the start-up of four new newsprint machines there, the country will again become a net importer of newsprint within two years.

Abitibi-Consolidated will have an annual capacity of 1.5 million tonnes of uncoated groundwood paper and 2.9 million tonnes of newsprint, making it the world's largest newsprting producer by a wide margin. It will have 18 paper mills, including 14 in Canada, three in the United States and one in the United Kingdom.

Doughan, and Ron Oberlander, chairman and chief executive officer of Abitibi-Price, who would become chairman of the merged company, said management will conduct an intensive review of each mill and machine as well as grade mix, capacity and capital expenditures. But both men declined to offer specifics on any asset sales or mill closures being mulled.

Doughan indicated that under the merger agreement, Stone Container Corp, which owns 46.6 percent of Stone-Consolidated and would own about 25 percent of Abitibi-Consolidated, has the right to buy additional stock in the merged company to prevent a hostile takeover.
Doughan said although such a takeover attempt of the merged company would be "highly unlikely," Stone Container could increase its holding to below 50 percent, but enough to block such a bid.
"They will never have the right to sell to a predator or a takeover. If they sell a block to anyone, it will be to someone who is not a predator," Doughan said.

The two men said a decision will be made in the coming weeks on closing one of the merging companies' head offices, but they ruled out moving the new head office to the United States. Abitibi-Price is based in Toronto, while Stone-Consolidated is based in Montreal.
